@Scotcheggs

As water droplets fall, they turn into parachute shapes and split once the surface tension/cohesion can't handle the wind forces hitting it. This repeats until it's small enough to reach a terminal velocity and make it to the ground.

As that process happens, more electrons get trapped in the upper atmosphere (relative to the storm) of the cloud by the constant "pummeling" of water droplets against each other and the wind while less electrons get to or near the ground. This keeps happening until enough charge difference between two points is built up that the system can correct itself and transfer all the built-up electrons in the air down to the electron-deprived lower (or sometimes equal) levels.

Electricity then finds the most efficient path to do that. Going through air is hard for electricity though because it's a terrible conductor. Water that is pure is also a very poor conductor. Water has to have minerals in it to be the great conductor the media (movies/video games) have us believe it is. Water falling out of a cloud is basically pure but picks up dust and stuff when it gets near the ground because it is condensing out of the cloud and water that has entered a gas phase (by way of evaporation) then re-entered the liquid phase has left behind it's impurities.

So all that comes together to make lightning. And why it seems so erratic.
